section.title: Torsion and the Frenet frame
section.p: measured how strongly a curve bends. Curvature records bending, but a curve in space has another freedom: it can twist out of the plane in which it is currently bending.

A circle and a helix show the missing information. The circle
\mathbf c(t) = \left(\frac52\cos t,\frac52\sin t,0\right)
has curvature \kappa=\frac{1}{5/2}=\frac25. The helix from , \mathbf h(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t), also has curvature \kappa=\frac25. Yet the two curves are plainly different. The circle is contained in one plane. The helix is not contained in any plane.
Curvature sees their equal bending. It does not see the helix's twisting. To measure that second effect, we first complete the tangent and normal vectors to a moving orthonormal frame.

subsection.title: The binormal and the osculating plane
subsection.p: For the rest of this section, let \mathbf r(s) be a regular curve in \mathbb R^3, parametrized by arc length, and suppose \kappa(s)>0. Then the unit tangent and unit normal vectors are defined, and \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N. The vectors \mathbf T and \mathbf N are perpendicular unit vectors. Their cross product gives a third perpendicular unit vector: \boxed{\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N.}

definition.title: Binormal, osculating plane, and Frenet frame

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(s) be a regular space curve with \kappa(s)>0.
The unit binormal vector is \boxed{\mathbf B(s)=\mathbf T(s)\times\mathbf N(s).}
The plane through \mathbf r(s) spanned by \mathbf T(s) and \mathbf N(s) is called the osculating plane. Its normal vector is \mathbf B(s).

subsection.p: The word osculating comes from a word meaning “kissing.” The tangent line follows the curve to first order. The osculating plane contains both the tangent direction and the first direction in which the tangent turns, so it follows the space curve one order more closely.

Because \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N, the Frenet frame is right-handed. Its cross products follow the same cyclic pattern as \mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k:
\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B, \qquad \mathbf N\times\mathbf B=\mathbf T, \qquad \mathbf B\times\mathbf T=\mathbf N.
Reversing the order reverses the sign. For example, \mathbf T\times\mathbf B=-\mathbf N. That sign will matter when we derive the formulas for the moving frame.

exercise.title: Why is the binormal perpendicular to the osculating plane?

statement.p: Explain why \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N is perpendicular to the osculating plane. Why does the order \mathbf T\times\mathbf N, rather than \mathbf N\times\mathbf T, matter?

hint.p: The osculating plane is spanned by \mathbf T and \mathbf N. Recall what the cross product does and how reversing its factors changes its sign.

figure.caption: The Frenet frame moves with the helix. The vectors \mathbf T and \mathbf N span the osculating plane, while \mathbf B is perpendicular to it. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The frame is attached to the curve, not to the fixed coordinate axes. As the point moves, the three vectors may all turn. Curvature tells how quickly \mathbf T turns. The turning of \mathbf B will measure how the osculating plane twists.

subsection.title: Torsion: how the osculating plane turns
subsection.p: The derivative of \mathbf B has a surprisingly restricted direction.
First, \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf B=1. Differentiating with respect to arc length gives 2\mathbf B\cdot\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=0. Thus \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\perp\mathbf B.

Also, \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf T=0. Differentiate:
\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\cdot\mathbf T + \mathbf B\cdot\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds} =0.
Since \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N and \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf N=0, we get \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\cdot\mathbf T=0. Therefore d\mathbf B/ds is perpendicular to both \mathbf T and \mathbf B. The only remaining Frenet direction is \mathbf N. Hence \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds} must be a scalar multiple of \mathbf N.
The minus sign is a convention. With this convention, the standard upward right-handed helix has positive torsion.

Curvature is nonnegative because it is defined as a length. Torsion is signed. Its magnitude is \boxed{|\tau|=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\right\|.} Thus |\tau| measures how quickly the binormal, and therefore the osculating plane, turns per unit distance traveled. The sign distinguishes the two possible senses of twisting.
Like curvature, torsion has units \frac{1}{\text{length}}. A plane curve has a fixed binormal vector, so its torsion is zero wherever its Frenet frame is defined.

statement.p: Curvature is always nonnegative, while torsion may be positive or negative. Explain what is different about the two definitions and what geometric information the sign of torsion records.

hint.p: Curvature is defined using a norm. Torsion is defined as a signed coefficient in d\mathbf B/ds=-\tau\mathbf N.

subsection.title: The Frenet–Serret formulas
subsection.p: We now know how two vectors in the frame change: \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N, and \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf N. The derivative of \mathbf N is forced by these two formulas.
The three equations form one system.
The formulas separate two geometric effects.
The coefficient \kappa couples \mathbf T and \mathbf N. It records bending inside the osculating plane.
The coefficient \tau couples \mathbf N and \mathbf B. It records twisting of the osculating plane through space.

subsection.title: Computing the frame and torsion from any parameter
subsection.p: Arc length gives the cleanest definitions, but a curve is usually presented as \mathbf r(t). We now turn the geometric definitions into formulas that use the original parameter.

Let \sigma(t)=\|\mathbf r'(t)\| be the speed. Since \mathbf r'(t)=\sigma\mathbf T, we have
\mathbf r''(t) \amp= \sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}
\amp= \sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N.
Taking the cross product with \mathbf r'=\sigma\mathbf T gives
\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'' \amp= \sigma\mathbf T \times \bigl(\sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N\bigr)
\amp= \sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B.
When \kappa>0, this gives the binormal directly:
\boxed{ \mathbf B(t) = \frac{\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)} {\|\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\|}. }
Then \boxed{\mathbf N(t)=\mathbf B(t)\times\mathbf T(t).} The order matters. The cross product \mathbf T\times\mathbf B would give -\mathbf N.
Torsion has an equally compact formula.

proof.p:
We already found \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''=\sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B. Also, \mathbf r''=\sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N. Differentiate this expression with respect to t. Most resulting terms lie in the span of \mathbf T and \mathbf N. The only term that can have a binormal component comes from differentiating \mathbf N: \sigma^2\kappa\frac{d\mathbf N}{dt}. By the chain rule and the Frenet–Serret formula,
\frac{d\mathbf N}{dt} \amp= \frac{d\mathbf N}{ds}\frac{ds}{dt}
\amp= \bigl(-\kappa\mathbf T+\tau\mathbf B\bigr)\sigma.
Therefore the binormal component of \mathbf r''' is \sigma^3\kappa\tau\mathbf B. Taking the dot product with \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''=\sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B gives (\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''=\sigma^6\kappa^2\tau. On the other hand, \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2=\sigma^6\kappa^2. Dividing gives the formula for \tau.

subsection.p: The scalar triple product in the numerator is signed volume. Thus the torsion formula has a geometric memory of orientation: the sign changes when the twisting changes from one handedness to the other.

remark.title: A practical computation order
remark.p:
For a C^3 curve with \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\ne\mathbf 0, compute
\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathbf T \amp= \frac{\mathbf r'}{\|\mathbf r'\|},\\ \mathbf B \amp= \frac{\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''} {\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|},\\ \mathbf N \amp= \mathbf B\times\mathbf T,\\ \kappa \amp= \frac{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|} {\|\mathbf r'\|^3},\\ \tau \amp= \frac{(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''} {\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2}. \end{aligned} }

subsection.title: The circular helix revisited
subsection.p: The helix from now gives a complete example.

example.title: The Frenet frame and torsion of a helix

statement.p:
Let \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t). We already know that \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt5 and \kappa=\frac25. The first three derivatives are \mathbf r'(t)=(-2\sin t,2\cos t,1), \mathbf r''(t)=(-2\cos t,-2\sin t,0), and \mathbf r'''(t)=(2\sin t,-2\cos t,0). Also, \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)=(2\sin t,-2\cos t,4). The numerator in the torsion formula is
(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r''' \amp= (2\sin t,-2\cos t,4) \cdot (2\sin t,-2\cos t,0)
\amp= 4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t
\amp= 4.
The denominator is
\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2 \amp= 4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+16
\amp= 20.
Therefore \boxed{\tau=\frac4{20}=\frac15.}

We can check the torsion sign directly. Differentiate \mathbf B:
\frac{d\mathbf B}{dt} = \frac1{\sqrt5}(\cos t,\sin t,0).
Since \frac{ds}{dt}=\sqrt5, we have
\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds} \amp= \frac{d\mathbf B/dt}{ds/dt}
\amp= \frac15(\cos t,\sin t,0)
\amp= -\frac15\mathbf N.
Thus the defining equation \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf N indeed gives \tau=\frac15.

The circle of radius 5/2 and this helix have the same curvature, \kappa=\frac25, but their torsions are different:
\text{circle:}\amp\qquad \tau=0, \text{helix:}\amp\qquad \tau=\frac15.
Curvature separates straightness from bending. Torsion separates planar bending from spatial twisting.

subsection.p:
More generally, the circular helix
\mathbf r(t)=(a\cos t,a\sin t,bt), \qquad a>0,
has
\boxed{ \kappa=\frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \qquad \tau=\frac{b}{a^2+b^2}. }
Changing the sign of b reverses the handedness of the helix and changes the sign of \tau, while \kappa remains unchanged.

subsection.title: Zero torsion and plane curves
subsection.p: The motivating circle had zero torsion, while the helix did not. Under the hypotheses needed for the Frenet frame, this is the exact distinction between planar and genuinely spatial curves.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(s) be a C^3 regular curve on a connected interval, parametrized by arc length, and suppose \kappa(s)>0 throughout the interval. Then the image of \mathbf r lies in a fixed plane if and only if \tau(s)=0 throughout the interval.

proof.p: Suppose first that the curve lies in a fixed plane. Let \mathbf b be a fixed unit normal to that plane. Both \mathbf T and \mathbf N lie in the plane, so \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N is either \mathbf b or -\mathbf b. Because \mathbf B varies continuously on a connected interval, it cannot jump from one choice to the other. Thus \mathbf B is constant. Hence \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=\mathbf 0, so \tau=0.

Conversely, suppose \tau=0. The third Frenet–Serret formula gives \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=\mathbf 0. Therefore \mathbf B is a fixed vector. Since \frac{d\mathbf r}{ds}=\mathbf T and \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf B=0, we have
\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(\mathbf r(s)\cdot\mathbf B\bigr) \amp= \mathbf T(s)\cdot\mathbf B
\amp= 0.
Thus \mathbf r(s)\cdot\mathbf B=c for some constant c. This is the equation of one fixed plane with normal \mathbf B. The entire curve lies in that plane.

subsection.p: The curvature assumption cannot simply be erased.

statement.p: Consider the straight line \mathbf r(s)=(s,0,0). It is certainly planar, and its curvature is \kappa=0. But \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\mathbf 0, so the curve does not choose a principal normal \mathbf N. Without \mathbf N, the binormal \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N and the torsion are not defined by the Frenet construction.
The theorem assumes \kappa>0 not because a straight line is somehow nonplanar, but because the Frenet frame itself needs a direction in which the tangent is turning.

subsection.p:
Curvature and torsion now give two independent rates:
\text{curvature }\kappa = \text{bending per unit length},
\text{torsion }\tau = \text{signed twisting per unit length}.
The Frenet–Serret equations show how these two scalar functions control the motion of the entire moving frame. A deeper theorem of curve geometry says that, when \kappa>0, the functions \kappa(s) and \tau(s) determine a space curve up to a translation and rotation. In that sense, curvature and torsion together are a geometric fingerprint of the curve.

aside.title: Looking ahead
aside.p: The Frenet frame moves because the curve bends and twists. uses a different moving frame, the polar vectors \mathbf e_r and \mathbf e_\theta, which move because the coordinate directions themselves change. In both cases, the same lesson returns: when a basis moves, its derivatives carry geometric information.
